title: Parallel web search is free on AI Gateway and eve through January 31
raw_summary: Parallel web search in fast mode is now free on AI Gateway through January 31, 2027, and Parallel is now the default web search for eve agents. The tool works with any AI Gateway model, with no separate Parallel API key. Parallel finds relevant web pages and returns links with short excerpts. You can filter results by website or publication date. In eve, the built-in web_search tool uses Parallel fast mode automatically when the model is served through AI Gateway. See the eve documentation for other search configurations. To use Parallel fast mode with the AI SDK, add gateway.tools.parallelSearch({ mode: 'fast' }) to your tools: The offer covers fast mode only, with Zero Data Retention enabled by default. Other modes are billed at standard pricing. Learn more in the web search documentation . Read more

title: Introducing Vercel X
raw_summary: Today we’re launching Vercel X , a six-week accelerator for AI founders at the idea and pre-seed stages. Join a cohort of 40 teams at our San Francisco HQ and build alongside Vercel’s product leaders, designers, and engineers. The program takes no equity for participation and offers access to a program-wide pool of more than $9M in credits from Vercel, AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI, and other partners. Applications are now open through November 29, 2026. The program runs from January 19 to March 2, 2027. Vercel has worked with more than 100 early-stage teams from around the world across three accelerator cohorts. Alumni include Rex , Alloy Robotics, Interfaze , Cervo , and Hacktron . Interfaze and Rex are backed by Y Combinator, and Cervo was acquired by Altana Technologies. Why Vercel X? If you’re applying to Vercel X, you probably have an idea or project you haven’t been able to stop thinking about. The next stretch is figuring out exactly what you’re building and who it’s for. We think you get through that stretch the Vercel way: by deeply understanding your customers, shipping quickly, and iterating to greatness. The program includes: Technical mentorship: Hands-on workshops and product feedback from Vercel’s design, product, and engineering teams. Partner credits: Put credits toward hosting, compute, and model API usage as you build and test your product. Founder community: A cohort of AI founders at the same stage, with weekly fireside chats featuring industry leaders. Investor access: Mentorship from VC partners and the opportunity to present your company to investors, ecosystem partners, and the Vercel community at Demo Day. Winning teams receive funding from Vercel Ventures and prizes from program partners. Who should apply We’re looking for technical builders with ambitious ideas and insatiable curiosity. You don’t need a finished product or traction. Tell us what you want to build, who needs it, what AI makes possible, and why you’re the right person or team for the job. Solo founders and teams of up to three can apply from around the world. You must be a Vercel customer and must not have participated in a traditional VC accelerator or raised an institutional seed round. See the additional eligibility requirements below. All participants must spend the full six weeks in San Francisco and attend weekly events in person. Apply to Vercel X Applications close at 11:59 p.m. PT on Sunday, November 29, 2026. Decisions will be released in mid-December. Apply to Vercel X → Applicants must be Vercel customers at or above the age of majority in their jurisdiction, able to commit to the full six weeks in person, and not located in or otherwise subject to restrictions imposed by U.S. sanctions laws. Vercel X program applications will be judged on the quality of the submission, the founder's background, and the overall potential for impact. Read more

title: Vercel Drives now reads files up to 6x faster
raw_summary: Vercel Drives now reads files up to 6x faster. The update improves cold-read performance. A new read-ahead algorithm uses your application’s access patterns to load data from persistent storage before it’s needed, reducing the time your code spends waiting. All drives get this update automatically, with no SDK upgrade or configuration changes required. Read pricing is unchanged. Learn more in the Vercel Drives documentation . Read more

title: Single-second static deployments now support more assets
raw_summary: Instant deployments let you deploy eligible static sites to Vercel in about a second, without a build step. They now support CSS, images, fonts, and other assets alongside HTML and Markdown. Deploy a landing page with its stylesheet and images, or a report created by your coding agent, through the Vercel CLI or REST API . With the CLI, run: Newly supported file types include: Styles and data: CSS, JSON, XML, plain text, and web manifests Images: SVG, PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, and ICO Fonts: WOFF, WOFF2, TTF, OTF, and EOT Documents and media: PDF, MP4, WebM, MP3, WAV, and OGG Instant deployments support up to 100 files totaling 25 MB or less. Vercel detects eligible deployments automatically, with no configuration required. Deployments that exceed these limits, include JavaScript or other unsupported files, or are triggered by Git still build as before. The same applies to projects with a framework preset, custom build settings, a root-level package.json or Vercel configuration file such as vercel.json , or a public/ directory. This update is rolling out across all plans. Learn more in the deployment documentation . Read more

title: Standard builds move to usage-based billing for new teams
raw_summary: Starting today, new Pro and Enterprise teams no longer include a Standard build slot. This brings Standard builds under the same usage-based billing model as other build machines. On Pro, Standard builds cost $0.014 per build minute, and your monthly usage credit applies to build usage. Enterprise rates follow your contract. Standard builds remain billable after switching from Elastic to Standard for teams covered by this change. Select a build machine in team settings or project settings , or read more about managing your builds . Read more

title: Vercel Blob now supports TTLs for automatic deletion
raw_summary: Vercel Blob can now delete blobs automatically. Pass ttlDays when you write a blob and it is deleted that many days after upload, from 1 to 730 days. The TTL counts from the blob's upload date. Use TTLs for blobs you would otherwise delete yourself, such as session transcripts, exports, and temporary uploads. ttlDays works on put() , copy() , putImage() , multipart uploads, and presigned upload URLs. Every write result and head() response now includes expiresAt , so you know when a blob is due for deletion. setTtl() changes or removes the TTL of blobs you already have, one URL or up to 1,000 at a time, without re-uploading them. In Vercel CLI 65.16.0 and later, pass --ttl-days to vercel blob put , put-image , copy or presign , and use vercel blob set-ttl on existing blobs. Setting a TTL costs one Advanced Operation per started 60 days, on top of the write. A 7-day TTL costs one, and the 730-day maximum costs 13. Clearing a TTL and the deletions themselves are free. You can track TTL operations in the Blob section of the Observability tab. npm install @vercel/blob@2.9.0 Learn more in the Vercel Blob documentation . Read more

title: Speed Insights now measures soft navigations
raw_summary: Speed Insights now measures soft navigations: client-side route changes that update page content without a full reload. This means you can now track performance as users move through your app, not just on full-page loads. Speed Insights captures LCP, FCP, INP, and CLS for soft navigations and includes these measurements in your Real Experience Score. TTFB is not captured because there is no new document request. Soft-navigation tracking is enabled by default for all projects using Speed Insights, with no action required. It works with modern web frameworks such as Next.js, SvelteKit, and Nuxt, in Chromium-based browsers. In your project's Speed Insights dashboard , use the new Navigation Type filter to view All , Hard , or Soft navigation data. Soft-navigation events count toward Speed Insights Plus usage. For existing projects that had Plus enabled before this release, Speed Insights events from soft navigations will not be charged until December 1. For projects that newly enable Plus, these events are billed from the start. To disable soft-navigation tracking, set softNavs to false in your application code and redeploy. This option requires @vercel/speed-insights version 2.1.0 or later: Learn more in the Speed Insights documentation . Read more

title: Pull-request-only preset now available for preview builds
raw_summary: A new Ignored Build Step preset lets you skip preview builds for branches without an open pull request. Production deployments and previews for branches with open pull requests continue to build. On GitHub and GitLab projects, skipped preview deployments are canceled before consuming any Build CPU Minutes. To enable this, open your project’s Deployments > Configuration . Under Ignored Build Step , select Only build previews for pull requests from the Behavior menu and click Save . Learn more in the Ignored Build Step documentation . Read more

title: Introducing eve 1.0
raw_summary: Today we're announcing eve 1.0 , the open-source framework for building production-ready agents. Since the public preview in June , we've worked with early adopters to prepare eve for 1.0, shipping 230+ releases and merging thousands of pull requests. With this release, eve is now generally available. We've made eve faster, expanded integrations, and improved observability. Security controls let you decide which actions need approval and what data gets collected. We've also made it easier for coding agents to build with, measuring that experience with a rigorous evaluation suite. With eve handling your harness and infrastructure, you and your agent can focus on building instead. Build production agents on a harness you own The harness in eve is the loop that calls models, runs tools, and delegates work to subagents. You choose the model, add or replace tools, edit instructions, and decide which actions need approval. The open-source Workflow SDK saves progress as the agent runs, so it can pick up from its last completed step after a crash. Multiplayer sessions and agent-to-agent calls are built in. For managed hosting, deploy your eve agent to Vercel. Vercel Workflows handles durable execution, and Vercel Sandbox runs agent-generated code in isolation. Build software factories that turn requests into tested pull requests, company brains that answer questions from your business data, or customer-facing agents in your product. Thousands of businesses already run eve in production for internal and customer-facing agents. Rillet built a software factory on eve that takes in customer requests, converts them into specs, tests the changes, and opens PRs for human review. Rillet tripled its shipping rate in three months. Clay built monty, a data agent that answers employees’ questions in Slack. Just over two months in, 30–40% of the company used it every week. Lindy 's agent framework roundup names eve “Best for durable backend agents”. Collaborate in multiplayer agent sessions Multiplayer lets several people work with an agent in one shared session. eve keeps track of who said what and directs approvals and sign-ins to the right person. You can set up memory for each user or the whole team. In the native Slack channel , each thread is one shared session. Approvals appear as buttons that only the right person can answer, and a live task card shows progress and timing. You can follow up in the thread without mentioning the agent again, cancel the current turn, or reset the session from Slack. Ambient mode lets an agent listen in channels you choose, even without being mentioned. Guided by goals you set per channel, it decides when to speak up, help, or take on a task, and when to stay quiet. To limit model costs, a small decision model screens every message first, and only the ones that might be for the agent start a turn. Slack is one of several native channels, alongside Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, GitHub, Linear, Twilio, Web Chat, and iMessage. The Chat SDK channel adds support for any Chat SDK platform adapter, including WhatsApp, Messenger, Google Chat, and email. Each channel is one file, and the same agent can work across all of them. See the integrations directory for the full list. Build agent UIs with Next.js and other frameworks eve 1.0 expands our native integrations for Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, TanStack Start, and Vite. The framework integrations build your agent alongside your app and set up its routes. On Vercel, you can deploy the agent and your site as one project, or host them separately. The client libraries let you work with tool calls, approval requests, and questions in a consistent way across frameworks. Use that session data to build custom UIs: stream replies into agent chats, embed an agent in a page, or show the agent's tool calls in your own components. Use eve add channel/web to scaffold a chat app with AI Elements components, or add eve's React, Vue, or Svelte bindings to an existing UI. Build multi-tenant agents One support-agent deployment can connect to each customer's ticketing system with their own credentials and apply that customer's approval rules. Your application authenticates the user and identifies which tenant they belong to. You can then set memory , connection credentials , and approval policy for that tenant and user. Before each model call in the main agent loop, dynamic definitions load the agent's capabilities from the session and external data. In 1.0, they cover models, connections, and subagents as well as tools, skills, and instructions. Give agents memory across sessions We added native memory so agents can carry context from one session to the next. You choose the memory's scope and can use the built-in file memory, a memory provider, or one you build yourself . Built-in fileMemory keeps data in memory in eve dev and in a private Vercel Blob store you configure on Vercel. Other providers include claude-mem , Hindsight , Kybernesis Arcana , Memanto , memco , Supermemory , and Upstash AgentKit . Trace agents with OpenTelemetry We rebuilt eve’s tracing around OpenTelemetry , so you can follow an agent’s work in the tracing tools you already use. eve dev records traces locally by default. If you host eve yourself, you can export them to an OpenTelemetry backend, including one you run yourself. Tracing integrations include Raindrop , with more options in the integrations directory . Add one with eve add instrumentation/<name> , or use the instrumentation APIs to build your own integration. Traces now show when an agent is waiting for a person, including tool approvals, questions, budget prompts, and sign-ins. They record model selections and approval decisions alongside model usage and cost, and follow calls into MCP servers and remote agents. You choose what eve collects for tracing. Content you exclude from collection stays out of every destination. You can filter out spans or redact inputs and outputs per destination. Private conversations in production send only metadata by default, without prompts or tool results. The OpenTelemetry guide explains these controls. On Vercel, Agent Runs uses the same traces to show sessions, model calls, tool execution, subagent activity, and approval decisions in the dashboard. When eve deploy creates a new Vercel project, it sets up trace sampling automatically. See the Agent Runs guide for setup and configuration. Lower agent turn latency At the start of September, our hosted stress test on Vercel Workflows took a median of 3.036s per turn . In 1.0, the same 100-turn workload took 414ms . The test sends messages one at a time, with one immediate mock-model response and no tool calls per turn. We measure from sending a message until the turn finishes, capturing eve and Workflow overhead without the time a model takes to generate a response. Hosted stress run Median turn latency p95 September 1, beta baseline 3.036s 3.692s November 15, 1.0.0 414ms 633ms We worked with the Workflow team on spec 9 , which gives each run a single orchestrator so background steps no longer replay the workflow. The team also moved event and stream writes to WebSockets and cut redundant history reads. eve agents get these improvements through Workflow SDK. eve also caches the information it needs to route messages to each session and can move idle sessions to a newer deployment between turns. Web UIs can prewarm a session before the first message arrives, so the first reply starts sooner. Lower workflow costs for long agent sessions For a 50-turn Evo Docs session, the estimated Vercel Workflows cost drops from 5.4¢ to 1.3¢, about 76% lower. That assumes roughly two model steps per turn and 30-day retention. eve now uses Workflow SDK 5.5 and saves only the conversation data that changed between turns. title: Agents are users, so your software needs evals
raw_summary: Agents are now users of software, doing work on people's behalf. Whether you're building the agent or the software it uses (API, CLI, MCP server, SDK), evals give you a way to measure how well that work gets done. Agents probably missed your launch video and billboard on Highway 101, but they still go through the same funnel a human does to find and use a product: Discovery , Selection , Access , and Success . You can build evals for any stage of this funnel. Here, we’ll focus on the final stage, Success : whether the agent completes the user’s task correctly. That's more difficult to check than it sounds. An agent can place a “successful” order for a hot latte when the user asked for an iced one. The request worked, so the logs in your Observability stack look fine. And because LLM outputs vary between runs, one good manual test can’t tell you whether a fix worked. You need to repeat the same tasks and grade the outcomes, before and after the change. That’s what an eval is, a test you run many times and score. Here’s how we build one. The agentic testing pyramid If a test asks “did it work?”, an eval asks “how often does it work, and how well?” We group agentic software tests by how many LLM calls they typically need: deterministic tests (0), one-turn evals (1), and E2E evals (2+ across a whole task). This has turned out to be a great proxy for the effort to build them, the time they take to run, and the cost of running them. Just like in the practical test pyramid , the cheap and fast tests should make up the bulk of your test suite. To use the pyramid, start with the problem you want to catch and pick the lowest tier that can catch it. For Success , that's the top. A one-turn eval checks a single decision, like which command the agent runs first. But Success depends on the whole sequence of steps (e.g. search for cafes → filter on user criteria → place the latte order). Each one can look reasonable on its own, and the agent can still get the wrong outcome. An E2E eval lets the agent work through the whole task in an environment, then checks whether the final result meets the user’s requirements. You’ve probably seen a few already; most popular coding benchmarks, like SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench , are E2E evals. Example Say you own SF Beans, an API for ordering coffee in San Francisco. One of the best ways to give agents access to your service is through a CLI, so you’re shipping sfbeans . Here’s a typical request from one of your customers: Get me a large iced latte with whole milk, ready for pickup by 9:00, under $8 including tip. I’m in the Mission. Here’s what sfbeans knows at 8:30am: Fog City Roasters: ice machine is down, so no iced drinks today (temperature) 24th St Beans: latte is $7.50 on the menu, but $9.27 after tax and tip (budget) Dolores Drip: latte is $5.50, but the earliest pickup is 9:20 (time) Valencia Grind: $7.42 after tax and tip, ready at 8:50 (meets all three) Here’s what you could test at each layer of the pyramid for sfbeans : How to build an end-to-end eval We’ll build the coffee eval with Harbor , an open-source framework from the creators of Terminal-Bench that runs agents in containers, checks results, and records their actions. Here are the terms we’ll use: Task : one problem for the agent to solve, with a starting environment and a way to check whether it succeeded Variant : the agent setup you’re testing, like the model, prompt, tools, memory and skills Trial : one attempt by one variant at one task Run (a job in Harbor): every variant tried on every task, several times each Trace (a trajectory in Harbor): everything recorded during a trial: messages, tool calls, logs, files and final output Step 1: Set a goal Building E2E evals for everything isn’t practical. With traditional software, you can aim for 100% test coverage. With agents, the surface you’d need to cover is everything an LLM might do with your product, and even figuring out where that ends is hard (see the jagged frontier ). Start with one outcome your users care about, narrow enough to evaluate with a handful of tasks. You’ll usually find that goal in one of three places: Observability: which agents use your product, and where they fail Customers: support tickets, feedback, and churn Roadmap: the product hypotheses you most need to validate For example, your goal might be to: Increase the success rate on a specific task Reduce the number of steps required to accomplish a goal Check whether an agent skill helps, and get feedback to improve it A/B test a prompt Explore the frontier by checking whether a use case is achievable with current LLMs, and if they fail, why Example We looked in all three places for sfbeans : Observability: Most agent traffic comes from Claude Code and Codex. We know because sfbeans adds a user-agent header when it detects a specific coding harness. Customers: The top support ticket is “my agent ordered the wrong drink”: a hot latte instead of iced, a pickup after the user’s meeting, or a total over budget once tax and tip are added. Roadmap: Nothing urgent, so the wrong-drink problem goes first, since it drives churn. That gives us our goal: Goal Increase the success rate on ordering the exact drink the user asked for Agents Claude Code and Codex, since that’s where our traffic comes from. In scope Drink, pickup time, and budget (incl. tax and tip), using today’s sfbeans . Out of scope Cancellations, refunds, and accounts. We’ll eval those later. Done when Both agents get the order right in every trial, not just most of the time. Step 2: Define metrics Here are the metrics we use most for E2E agent evals: Success Success rate: the share of trials that pass Pass@k : the chance that at least one of k trials passes (answers “can the agent do this at all?”) Pass^k : the chance that all k trials pass (answers “can I rely on it every time?”) Efficiency (measured on successful trials only) Steps: the number of agent turns needed to complete the task Time: how long the trial took Cost: how much the trial cost, in dollars Example Our goal is to get every order right in every trial. Once we build and run the eval in Steps 3 and 4, here’s what five trials of Claude Code + Opus 5.5 ( anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 on AI Gateway ) on the iced latte order could look like: Trial Result What happened Steps Time Cost 1 Pass Compared quotes from 3 cafes, ordered at Valencia 9 3:40 $0.52 2 Fail: over budget Skipped quote, ordered at 24th St: $9.27 5 1:50 $0.31 3 Pass Compared quotes from 4 cafes, ordered at Valencia 11 4:30 $0.68 4 Fail: late Ordered at Dolores, ready 9:20 6 2:10 $0.35 5 Pass Skipped Fog City, ordered at Valencia 8 3:20 $0.49 What the numbers mean: Success rate: 3 of 5 trials passed, so 60%. Pass@5: Assuming independent trials with a 60% success rate, 1 − 0.4^5 ≈ 99%. Give the agent 5 tries and it almost certainly gets it right once. Pass^5: 0.6^5 ≈ 8%. The chance the agent gets 5 orders in a row right. Steps: (9 + 11 + 8) / 3 ≈ 9 on successful trials. The failed trials are shorter because the agent skipped work, like quoting, which is why efficiency only counts successful trials. Time: ~3:50 on successful trials. Cost: $0.56 per successful trial, but $2.35 / 3 = $0.78 per success once you count the failed trials you paid for too. So does Opus work? Its 99% pass@5 says yes. Its 8% pass^5 says a user who orders this every weekday gets at least one wrong coffee in 92% of weeks. Both numbers are right. They just answer different questions: pass@5 asks whether the agent can get the order right, and pass^5 asks whether it gets it right every time . Which metric matters most depends on what a failure costs your user. Someone ordering their morning coffee doesn’t get a retry. If the agent orders a hot latte, or one that’s ready after their train leaves, they’ve paid for the wrong coffee and started their day annoyed. They need it right every morning, so sfbeans optimizes for pass^5. Other products are more forgiving, because a failed attemp…

title: Immigrants' skills and capital deepening: evidence from Chile
raw_summary: We study the effect of migration on firms’ capital deepening, leveraging a massive influx of immigrant workers with varying skill sets from Venezuela and Haiti in Chile between 2015 and 2019.

title: "Eppur si muove": convergence within and between countries
raw_summary: Kremer, Willis, and You (2022) report that over six decades richer countries lost their growth advantage. Acemoglu and Molina (2022) and Pesaran and Smith (2026) reply that such regressions cannot measure catch-up when countries head toward different moving destinations.

title: The gig economy and digital payments
raw_summary: The growth of the “gig” economy could have far-reaching implications for payment systems. Gig work involves digital platforms that intermediate between workers and (retail or business) customers, in areas as diverse as ride-hailing and food delivery, freelance design and professional services, and customer service.

title: Ready-to-run global liquidity stress tests for banks and banking systems
raw_summary: Liquidity risk remains a persistent threat to financial stability, as starkly demonstrated by the 2023 banking turmoil in the United States and Europe. Hence, the ability to quickly gauge banks’ liquidity risks could prove useful especially during periods of market stress, but also to assess differences in liquidity buffers across peer economies and banks.

title: US monetary policy, macroeconomic news and the global secular decline of interest rates
raw_summary: The global secular decline in long-term interest rates since the 1990s has been largely driven by cumulative yield changes during U.S. monetary policy announcement windows (FOMC windows).

title: Gaining (and losing) currency: a global database of currencies, 1850-2026
raw_summary: Over the past two centuries, officially issued currencies have become firmly en trenched as a nearly universal institution in economies around the world. But the path to this arrangement has not been smooth: currencies have come and gone, in line with political changes, periods of hyperinflation or currency reforms and, in some cases, entry into currency unions.

title: Scenarios for future banking: implications for profitability, liquidity and solvency
raw_summary: Who will perform banking’s core functions a decade from now, and how will risks and profitability evolve? Our framework structures expert judgement rather than forecasts.

title: Refined slippage: variance reduction using counterfactual returns
raw_summary: A new metric is introduced that benchmarks fill prices against counterfactual prices, rather than the arrival price

title: Smile dynamics and rough volatility
raw_summary: The joint spot-smile dynamics is analysed through the skew stickiness ratio lens

title: Does the Stock Market Stigmatize Banks that Borrow from the Fed?
raw_summary: Banks may resist borrowing from the Federal Reserve during a panic if such borrowing is stigmatized (that is, viewed by the market as a sign of financial weakness), thus hampering the Fed’s ability to resolve the crisis. The problem may be particularly acute for publicly traded banks since their stock prices immediately reflect the market's opinion of them. In this post, based on a recent paper , we track what happened to stock investors' perceptions of a bank's risk level right after it first borrowed from Fed facilities in the first month of the bank run of 2023 . We find that, after a first trip to the Fed's Discount Window (DW), investors became more sensitive to that bank's weaknesses. In contrast, investors did not evince such concern when the bank took a first loan from a new facility, the Bank Term Funding Program (BTFP).

title: Can Workers Predict Job Finding and Job Loss?
raw_summary: Workers’ perceptions of the labor market may differ from aggregate labor market statistics. Individuals might be overly optimistic about their chance of finding a job, or too pessimistic about the odds of losing their current position. In this post, we compare subjective beliefs of future job-finding and job-loss from the New York Fed’s Survey of Consumer Expectations (SCE) with their realized counterparts in the Current Population Survey (CPS). We then investigate how closely aggregate perceptions of job-finding and job-loss prospects align with realized rates.

title: Banking System Vulnerability: 2026 Update
raw_summary: As in previous years, we provide in this post an update on the vulnerability of the U.S. banking system based on four analytical models that capture different aspects of this vulnerability. We use data through 2026:Q2 to update our analysis and discuss how the vulnerability measures have changed since our last update one year ago .

title: A Look at the Wider Divide in Credit Card Delinquency by Income
raw_summary: Credit card delinquency rose sharply between 2022 and 2024, and the increase was steepest among borrowers in lower-income neighborhoods. Here, we check in on credit card performance by neighborhood income and trace when the borrowers who are now struggling with their payments were issued cards. We find that during the pandemic, an increasing share of new credit cards went to borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores, and those accounts are now showing higher levels of distress.

title: Has U.S. Monetary Policy Really Improved? A 150‑Year Perspective
raw_summary: Has U.S. monetary policy actually improved over time? Or was the apparent success of the modern Federal Reserve mostly the result of more favorable economic conditions and better luck? In this post, we summarize our paper , * which develops a framework for comparing monetary policy across different economic environments. Our approach asks how close policy came to the best response given the economic conditions and shocks policymakers faced. Applying this framework to 150 years of U.S. monetary history, we find that meaningful improvements in monetary policy occurred only in the last thirty years. Most of the gains reflect, among other developments, substantially better responses to financial shocks and supply shocks.

title: The U.S. Oil Sector’s Role in Restraining Prices
raw_summary: The start of the Middle East conflict in early 2026 caused an unprecedented drop in global petroleum supply. In response, oil prices jumped—but not to unprecedentedly high levels. The U.S. oil sector was a key factor in moderating the shock. For one, its steady increases in drilling helped create a large oversupply in the global market before the conflict, making it less of a challenge to offset the drop in Middle East oil output. In addition, U.S. commercial and government inventories were rapidly drawn down, filling half the gap between global supply and demand in the second quarter by some estimates. Inventories, though, are a limited resource and U.S. stockpiles stopped falling in July. As a consequence, the continued shortfall in global production has been managed by running down inventories in the rest of the world.

title: How Market Position Shapes Credit Card Interest Rates
raw_summary: Why is it that two borrowers who look much alike can be offered very different rates when applying for a credit card? In a recent paper , we address this question by examining how the rate offered changes when the lender’s funding cost falls. Data on 14 million newly issued cards show that when a lender's funding costs decline, the lender passes less of that decline on to the offer rate when it holds a large market share. That is, two borrowers with similar credit scores and incomes borrowing from the same lender can see noticeably different interest rates on the credit card they are applying for.

title: AI, accountability and the economics of evidence
raw_summary: Benjamin Guin Most discussion of AI in organisations focuses on productivity: as analysis becomes cheaper, decision-making should improve. This post argues that an important consequence lies elsewhere. Where the relevant information is accessible, a wider range of people can produce professionally presented analysis and submit it to decision-makers. Responsibility for decisions, however, remains concentrated and … Continue reading AI, accountability and the economics of evidence →

title: FEDS Paper: Artificial Intelligence and the U.S. Economy: Current Evidence
raw_summary: Nick Carollo , Leland D. Crane , Daniel Garcia Molina , and Joseph Nichols We assess the current evidence on how AI-related investment and the use of AI are affecting the U.S. macroeconomy. Specifically, we document the boom in data center capital investment, the current rate of adoption of AI tools in the economy, the impact of the AI-related investment surge on prices, and discuss whether AI tools have affected the labor market and productivity yet. Driven by current and expected future demand for AI services, investment in data centers, both the physical structures and semiconductor chips and other IT equipment inside the structures, has climbed sharply. AI adoption is growing rapidly both among consumers and firms, though most firms are currently not using AI very intensively or at all. AI model-producing firms have also grown extremely fast, and now account for a noticeable fraction of software industry gross output. Prices have climbed in sectors that provide direct inputs to the data centers, such as memory chips. Effects on the labor market so far appear small and somewhat mixed. Similarly, the effects of AI on aggregate productivity growth also appear to be small so far, and the recent pickup in productivity likely reflects factors that predated the diffusion on generative AI.

title: FEDS Paper: Costly Misdemeanours: Labour Market Effects of Low-Level Drink-Driving Violations
raw_summary: Kabir Dasgupta , Marco Francesconi, Jonathan James Linda Kirkpatrick, and Alexander Plum This paper estimates the causal effect of a drink-driving conviction on labour market outcomes. Using linked administrative data and variation in the timing of first convictions in a staggered difference-in-differences design, we compare individuals before and after conviction to those convicted later. We find employment falls by 6–7 percentage points and monthly earnings decline by around 2 percent. The effects are driven primarily by reduced job entry as opposed to job loss. Employment effects are largest in industries where employers are more likely to screen applicants for criminal convictions.

title: A modern dilemma: Consume data from a stream or a lake
raw_summary: Data is a critical component of software architecture, providing the foundation for business processes, including those powered by artificial intelligence (AI). Quality, volume, latency, consistency, ordering and duplicates are essential considerations in software design. Modern cloud architectures consume data in various ways, such as through application programming interfaces (APIs), streams and data lakes. You can consume data at the individual event or record level as it arrives or in larger batches. Legacy architectures often process data in scheduled batches, forcing surrounding architecture and business processes to depend on that approach. Getting the data consumption approach right up front is vital, because rearchitecting later is costly. General patterns to consume data There are several general data consumption patterns. These include APIs (record-by-record or multirecord results), event stream consumption (record-by-record), Delta Change Data Feed (CDF) consumption (record-by-record) or traditional batch ETL-extract, transform, load (multirecord results). APIs are ideal for low-latency, record-by-record requirements. They also support multirecord results, typically through pagination. APIs usually follow a synchronous approach, where the client makes a call and waits for a response before moving to the next step. Model Context Protocol is an industry specification for agents to consume data and can support record-by-record or batch results via pagination, similar to APIs. They are often a wrapper on top of APIs. The event stream pattern works well for sub-second latency requirements and typically runs on a tech stack like Kafka, Flink or Spark Streaming. These technologies excel at record-level calculations (like on-the-fly calculation), transformations (like column mapping) or enrichment (like adding data to an existing event). Delta Lake is often used in data lakes and serves as a transaction log to standard Apache Parquet data files ( source ). CDF is a Delta Lake feature that tracks row-level changes (inserts, updates and deletes) between table versions ( source) . Delta CDF consumption is an alternative for handling record-level calculations compared to the event stream pattern, with a few key differences. Latency can still be low but rarely sub-second. The tech stack consists only of a Spark job and an Amazon S3 bucket, simplifying complexity and maintenance. This pattern provides higher cost efficiency for high-volume data. At extreme volumes (2 million per second), streaming can delay, especially during event replay. Traditional batch ETL handles record groups and performs joins across many source datasets. Similar to Delta CDF, Spark and S3 can implement batch ETL. The key difference is the presence of many more source and destination datasets. These jobs run at massive scale with significant compute power. Consistency, ordering and duplicates Many considerations inform data consumption design. Consistency is one of the first to be defined: Does your design need strong or eventual consistency? Strong consistency means the process requires a response before proceeding to get the current state as of that exact moment and is often blocking or synchronous. Eventual consistency means processing will eventually get a response and is asynchronous (nonblocking). See the illustration below for details. Strong consistency vs. eventual consistency Ordering Order is another important consideration. Do you need to consume data in the exact order it was produced, or does order not matter? It is essential to understand which technology patterns preserve the original order of the data so consumers can take appropriate action. Kafka, for example, does not guarantee order across partitions when using multiple partitions. Kafka ordering within a single partition vs. across multiple partitions Duplicates At-least-once delivery and exactly-once delivery describe the nature of duplicates. At-least-once delivery guarantees data delivery at least once, meaning it could arrive multiple times and result in duplicates. Exactly-once delivery guarantees the message will be delivered only once. Kafka Streams supports exactly-once delivery. Consumers need these details to set proper expectations and design processes appropriately. With at-least-once delivery patterns, producers can use data keys that enable consumers to deduplicate data. With data lakes, one approach to eliminating duplicate records is an upsert mode that checks keys to see whether a record already exists. If it does, the system updates it; if not, it inserts it. At-least-once vs. exactly-once delivery comparison Use case characteristics of consumption patterns We categorize our five general patterns into two buckets: traditional batch ETL processing and real-time processing (e.g., APIs, event streams, Delta CDF). The use case characteristics below inform when data should be consumed via batch or a real-time pattern. Traditional batch ETL processing Batch ETL processing executes against a large batch set of data rather than individual records as they arrive. The following use case characteristics are a good fit: Processing requires more than a day’s worth of historical data. This data is used within transformation logic, enabling sophisticated calculations, trend analysis and the derivation of insightful features based on historical patterns and context. Doing this in a stream takes longer and may not scale, depending on data volume. Processing requires an entire day’s worth of data. These use cases require collecting an entire dataset before processing to ensure data quality, consistency and adherence to downstream formats. Joining large datasets spanning large time windows. This performs efficient, scalable joins across extensive datasets, using optimized algorithms and distributed computing frameworks to handle complex relationships without compromising performance. Real-time processing (e.g., APIs, event stream, Delta CDF) Real-time processing requires immediate data handling and transformation as it arrives, enabling timely insights and actions. The following use case characteristics are a good fit: Executing row-level transformations. This involves applying specific functions or logic to individual data records upon ingestion. Transformations can include data cleansing, standardization, enrichment or the creation of derived fields. This granular processing ensures data accuracy and prepares it for subsequent analysis or integration. Performing data transformations upon API calls. This allows dynamic data manipulation based on external information retrieved through API interactions. As real-time data arrives, the system makes a call to an external service to fetch additional context or perform specific processing steps. These API results further transform incoming data, enabling richer processing. Initiating real-time API calls based on incoming data streams. This feature enables the immediate application of logic or models when receiving incoming data streams. By invoking inference APIs in real time, organizations generate predictions, classifications or anomaly detections as events occur. This is vital for proactive decision-making, personalized experiences and automated responses. Executing real-time joins between a data stream and a static dataset. This join combines a continuously flowing stream of real-time data with a relatively unchanging dataset. This enriches streaming data with reference information, such as looking up customer details, product information or geographical location. The static nature of one dataset allows efficient, rapid lookups during real-time processing.
